title: 22. Associations among growth performance, gas exchange, and residual index traits of receiving beef heifers.
content:
Abstract
The beef industry must improve efficiency while also addressing environmental concerns related to greenhouse gas emissions. Residual index traits have been developed to identify cattle with lower dry matter intake (DMI) or emissions than expected; however, further research is needed to better understand how these traits relate to growth performance and greenhouse gas emissions. The objective of this study was to evaluate their associations with residual index traits in receiving heifers. Crossbred beef heifers (n = 28; initial BW = 369 ± 21 kg) were adapted for 14 d to Vytelle SENSE™ feed intake measurement bunks (Vytelle LLC, Lenexa, KS) and had been acclimated to a GreenFeed emission monitoring system (C-Lock Inc., Rapid City, SD) in a previous study for the measurement of methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide emissions and oxygen consumption. These gas fluxes were then used to calculate heat production (HP). Cattle were fed a sorghum silage-based grower ration (1.45 Mcal NEm/ kg) for 42 d, then transitioned to a corn silage-based grower ration (1.65 Mcal NEm/ kg) for the final 14 d, for a total of 56 d. Residual indexes evaluated included residual feed intake (RFI), residual methane production (RMP), and residual heat production (RHP). Each residual trait was calculated as the difference between predicted and observed values relative to metabolic body weight and DMI for RFI and RMP, and metabolic body weight, average daily gain, and DMI for RHP. Residual feed intake was negatively correlated (r = -0.58; P < 0.01) with methane yield (g CH4 per kg DMI; MY), meaning that more feed efficient cattle emitted more CH4 per unit of DMI. This relationship is largely driven by RFI and DMI being positively correlated (r = 0.61; P < 0.01) and DMI having a negative relationship with MY (r = -0.53; P < 0.01). The RMP trait was positively correlated with CH4 (r = 0.67), MY (r = 0.76), and RHP (r = 0.62). These relationships suggest that selecting cattle for RMP may reduce CH4 production and increase energetic efficiency of cattle. Residual heat production was positively correlated with CH4 production (r = 0.40; P = 0.04) and MY (r = 0.48; P = 0.01). Cattle with low RHP values produce less heat production than their cohorts for their given body weight, level of DMI, and ADG. Accordingly, low RHP cattle may be more energetically efficient than high RHP cattle. None of the residual traits were significantly related towards feeding behavior of the cattle, except for a tendency (P = 0.09) for meal eating rate and RFI to be positively related (r = 0.33). These results indicate that cattle can be identified for feed and energetic efficiency while reducing enteric CH4 emissions in confinement.
